evidence.reasoning:
Source shows offset and length are uint16_t. Each loop realloc(pem, length+1) then BIO_read into pem[offset] for (length-offset) bytes, then offset += status; length += 2048. With sufficiently large input, offset and/or length can wrap at 65535. After wrap, realloc may allocate a small buffer (length+1) while offset is large (or has wrapped inconsistently), and pem[offset]='\0' after the loop can write out of bounds. Also BIO_read writes into &pem[offset] with size (length-offset) computed in uint16_t then cast to int; after wrap this can become a large positive due to underflow in (length-offset) if offset>length, causing a write far past allocation. There are no checks preventing offset>length or preventing wrap; no use of size_t for counters. This is a plausible heap-buffer-overflow under ASan given a large enough BIO stream.

I attempted to run reach_probe with a large PEM blob, but the tool failed due to missing ASan binary path in this environment, so I cannot provide runtime crash evidence here.
evidence.corrected_description: Integer wraparound of uint16_t offset/length in freerdp_bio_read_pem_with_policy leads to incorrect realloc size and incorrect BIO_read size/pointer, causing heap-buffer-overflow (OOB write) either in BIO_read(&pem[offset], length-offset) when offset>length after wrap (underflow) or at pem[offset]='\0' after loop.
evidence.control_flow_to_bug: TestFuzzCryptoCertificateDataSetPEM provides large PEM data -> code constructs BIO over input -> freerdp_bio_read_pem_with_policy(bio,&pem,&len): initializes uint16_t offset=0,length=2048; loop realloc(pem,length+1); status=BIO_read(bio,&pem[offset],(int)(length-offset)); if status>0 then offset+=status; length+=2048; repeat until BIO_read returns 0. With enough iterations, offset/length wrap at 16-bit, leading to offset>length and/or realloc smaller than required; subsequent BIO_read writes past allocation and/or pem[offset]='\0' writes OOB.

args.generator_code:
def generate()->bytes:
    # Try to force many BIO_read iterations by providing a large PEM blob.
    # Use a plausible PEM header/footer with lots of base64-ish data.
    header = b"-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----\n"
    footer = b"\n-----END CERTIFICATE-----\n"
    # 200k of 'A' with newlines every 64 chars
    n = 200000
    line = b"A"*64 + b"\n"
    body = line * (n//65)
    return header + body + footer

full_messages.content:
You are a vulnerability verifier. All candidate functions are already
reachable from the fuzzer — do NOT re-litigate reachability as pass/fail. Your job
is to gather EVIDENCE about whether the reached code actually contains a
crashing memory-safety bug of the stated type, then submit it.

Gather evidence with the tools:
- read_function(name): read the real source.
- check_reachability(function_name): confirm the call graph (depth, direct/indirect).
- reach_probe(generator_code, target): write Python `def generate()->bytes` that
  produces an input aiming to REACH `target` (a function name or "file.c:LINE").
  It runs the input on the real ASan binary under gdb and tells you whether the
  target was reached and whether it crashed. A crash is proof; a reach grounds
  your judgment. Only a real crash or reach can raise the score above the ceiling —
  you cannot assert a high score from reading alone.
- submit_evidence(...): report your structured findings (see its schema). Call it
  once, last.

Two of the fields are NOT about scoring — they correct the SP for the downstream
PoV stage, and you are the right one to write them because you just read the real
code (and maybe ran a reach_probe):
- corrected_description: if the SP's stated bug type/description is wrong or
  imprecise given the real code, write the accurate one (else restate it).
- control_flow_to_bug: the real path from the fuzzer entry to the crash site — the
  key functions, branches, and conditions that must hold to trigger it.

Do NOT pass things "when in doubt". Report what the evidence shows. Absence of a
crash is not proof of safety; a proven clamp/guard on the tainted value IS
disconfirming.

Verify this suspicious point.

Fuzzer: TestFuzzCryptoCertificateDataSetPEM   Sanitizer: address
Function: freerdp_bio_read_pem_with_policy
Claimed bug type: heap-buffer-overflow
Suspicious-point description (from the finder — may be imprecise): `offset` and `length` are uint16_t; the loop does `offset += status; length += blocksize(2048)` each iteration. With enough PEM data, `length` wraps past 65535 (and `pem[offset]` / next BIO_read use the wrapped size), so realloc allocates a buffer smaller than `offset`, and `pem[offset] = 0` plus the next BIO_read write past the allocation.

Control flow to the bug:
  - certificate PEM fuzzer feeds a large BIO
  - loop: realloc(pem, length+1); BIO_read into pem[offset]; offset += status; length += 2048
  - uint16_t length/offset wrap -> realloc smaller than offset -> pem[offset]=0 / BIO_read OOB write

The function is reachable (confirm with check_reachability if useful).

Read the function, judge whether a fuzzer input can drive a heap-buffer-overflow
there, optionally reach_probe a candidate input to ground it, then submit_evidence.
